content: The disagreements during the study were resolved through consensus. The risk of bias in the included studies was assessed using version 2 of the Cochrane Risk-of-Bias Tool for Randomized Trials (RoB 2). For cluster-randomized trials, additional assessments were made regarding the timing of participant identification or recruitment, while for cross-over trials, potential period and carryover effects were evaluated. The overall risk of bias for each trial was determined based on the least favorable assessment across these domains. For dichotomous data, results were presented as risk ratios (RRs) or odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Results from cluster-randomized and individually randomized studies were combined, with cluster-randomized studies labeled accordingly. When trial authors adjusted for clustering effects, the cluster-adjusted RR and standard error were extracted and analyzed using the generic inverse variance method in Review Manager (RevMan). If clustering adjustments were not made, crude RRs and 95% CIs were calculated, and clustering effects were accounted for using an approximate analysis method, inflating the standard error of the RR based on the design effect. Sensitivity analyses were conducted to explore the potential effects of clustering on confidence intervals. For outcomes with skewed data, such as ferritin and retinol, log-transformed data were used for meta-analysis. In studies with more than two intervention groups, only directly relevant arms were included in the analysis, ensuring each group was analyzed only once. Heterogeneity was assessed by examining methodological and clinical differences between studies, including participant types, interventions, and outcomes. Statistical heterogeneity was quantified using the I² statistic. Funnel plots were used to assess reporting bias, and Egger’s test was applied to quantify funnel plot asymmetry when at least 10 studies were included in a meta-analysis. A random-effects model was used to combine data when clinical differences between studies were expected, providing an average treatment effect across studies. Subgroup analyses were planned to investigate potential sources of clinical heterogeneity, including age groups, types of nutrients added through fortification, types of fortified products, intervention duration, country income classification, baseline anemia status, and funding sources (industry vs. academic). Sensitivity analyses were also conducted to examine the effects of clustering on summary estimates. The certainty of evidence was rated using the GRADE approach, considering risk of bias, indirectness, inconsistency, imprecision, and publication bias. A total of 15,496 unique records were identified through database searches, and after removing duplicates, 8,313 records were screened based on titles and abstracts. Of these, 494 full-text records were assessed for eligibility, and 21 studies met the inclusion criteria, including 16 with full-text publications and 5 with unpublished results. The included studies involved 5,089 participants, with eight being individually randomized controlled trials (RCTs), one non-randomized controlled trial, and seven cluster-RCTs. Most studies were conducted in upper-middle-income or lower-middle-income countries, with only one study conducted in a high-income country (USA). Participants ranged in age from 6 to 60 months, and all studies included children of both sexes. Sample sizes varied from 40 to 1,465 participants. The interventions included fortified complementary foods, primarily cereals, with varying durations ranging from three feeding sessions to 18 months. Fortified products included wheat-based, maize/corn-based, rice-based, and legume-based foods, with fortification involving iron alone or combinations of micronutrients such as zinc, vitamin A, and others. Some studies used biofortification methods. Secondary outcomes included mental and motor skill development, morbidity, plasma vitamin E concentrations, and acceptability of fortified foods. Adverse effects, all-cause mortality, gut microbiota composition, and displacement of other foods were not reported in the included studies. Funding sources varied, with eight studies funded by government or non-commercial organizations, six funded partially or fully by commercial entities, and two not reporting funding sources. Five ongoing trials were identified but not yet published. The risk of bias was assessed for all included studies. Only two studies adequately described the randomization process, while others had concerns due to insufficient information or issues with allocation sequence concealment. Deviations from intended interventions, missing outcome data, and other biases were also noted in several studies. Overall, 50% of the studies were rated as having a high risk of bias. The review included 16 studies with 5,089 children, focusing primarily on anemia and hematological indices, with fewer studies reporting growth and developmental outcomes. Fortified complementary foods were found to reduce anemia by 43% and significantly increase hemoglobin and ferritin concentrations. However, no significant effects were observed on zinc or vitamin A status. Nutrient excess and stunting or wasting were not reported in the included studies. Acceptability of fortified foods was evaluated in three studies, with no significant differences in liking between fortified and non-fortified groups.
